messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Tama Faleolo is a 63-year-old Samoan-American man who works as a publisher in a mid-sized firm in Portland, Oregon. He has been married for thirty-one years and, until recently, was regarded by colleagues and family alike as steady, dependable, and warm. He presented for psychological assessment following what he described, with visible reluctance, as "months of not being able to function properly." His PCL-5 score of 79 places him in the severe range, and the clinical picture that emerged across intake and early sessions reflects a presentation firmly consistent with PTSD.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Tama was among a group of publishing industry professionals attending a waterfront conference in Seattle when an industrial explosion occurred at a nearby chemical storage facility. The blast sent a pressure wave through the conference hall, shattering glass and collapsing part of a mezzanine structure. In the chaos that followed, Tama found himself pinned briefly beneath debris, surrounded by smoke, screaming, and the sharp, acrid smell of accelerant — a smell he would later identify as resembling industrial alcohol. He watched a colleague lose consciousness metres away and was uncertain, in those minutes, whether the man was dead. Tama eventually freed himself and assisted in evacuating others before emergency services arrived. He was physically uninjured, which he has since used as a reason to minimise what happened to him.

In the weeks that followed the explosion, Tama noticed that his memories of the event had a quality unlike ordinary recollection. They were not summoned — they arrived. Vivid, pictorial, and uninvited, images of the collapsed mezzanine and the smoke-filled hall would force their way into his mind without warning, particularly when he was talking about the event with his wife or, on one occasion, a concerned colleague who asked directly what had happened. These intrusive visual memories began to feel dangerous to him in themselves, as though engaging with them would make something worse. That conviction — that the memories were a source of ongoing threat — drove him toward increasingly effortful avoidance: he stopped discussing the event entirely, declined social invitations where the topic might arise, and began withdrawing from the friends he had seen regularly for years. What had been a rich social life contracted sharply over the following months, and several friendships have quietly lapsed.

The sense of threat that took hold after the explosion did not remain confined to the memories. Tama came to feel, with a certainty that surprised and frightened him, that danger was present and ambient — even inside his own home. He began startling violently at ordinary sounds: a door closing, a truck passing outside his window, his wife setting down a pan in the kitchen. That persistent state of alarm fed directly into his behaviour at work. As a publisher, Tama attends editorial meetings, author events, and industry lunches regularly, and he has found himself unable to sit anywhere in a room unless his back is against a wall and the full space is visible to him. He scans every room he enters — the conference room at his office, the restaurant where his team holds quarterly lunches — before he can settle enough to concentrate. His assistant has noticed the habit, though nothing has been said directly.

The maintaining cycle that has come to define Tama's daily experience is one he cannot yet see clearly from the inside. His constant environmental scanning and positional vigilance keep his nervous system primed, which means that ordinary stimuli — a sudden sound, the smell of cleaning solvent that faintly recalls the accelerant from that day — land with the force of alarms and pull the visual memories forward again. The memories, once activated, confirm to him that the threat is real and unresolved, which tightens his surveillance further and deepens his avoidance of anything that might disturb the fragile equilibrium he has constructed. When he wakes from nightmares, the residue of those images sits with him through the morning, making the workday feel like a sustained exercise in containment.

What finally brought Tama to seek help was a conversation with his wife, who told him quietly one evening that she felt she had lost him. He is most afraid that she is right — and most hoping, though he struggles to say it plainly, that some version of the man he was before that afternoon in Seattle might still be recoverable.
